organism: Herpes zoster (shingles) is caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) - the same DNA herpesvirus that causes varicella on primary infection. After primary infection, VZV persists indefinitely, noninfectiously, in sensory nerve ganglia; the immunologic mechanism that controls this latency is not well understood, but recognized risk factors for reactivation include aging, immunosuppression, intrauterine VZV exposure, and having had varicella before 18 months of age.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Zoster presents as a vesicular eruption confined to a single dermatome (it does not cross the midline), most often on the trunk or face; pain and paresthesia in the area may precede the rash by 2-4 days. The rash lasts 7-10 days and heals in 2-4 weeks. Healthy people have few systemic symptoms; immunocompromised people can develop disseminated disease with central nervous system, pulmonary, and hepatic involvement. Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) - pain persisting in the rash area after the lesions resolve, sometimes for months or over a year - is the most common and debilitating complication and can be difficult to treat. Other complications include ophthalmic involvement, bacterial superinfection, cranial and peripheral nerve palsies, and visceral involvement.
epidemiologySummary: VZV is a human-only pathogen with no known animal or insect reservoir. It spreads via direct contact with vesicular fluid or inhalation of aerosols from skin lesions - but exposure to either varicella or zoster causes varicella, not zoster, in a susceptible contact; zoster itself is not 'caught' from someone else, only reactivated from a person's own prior infection. There is no seasonal pattern. A person with zoster is contagious from rash onset until the lesions crust, and is about one-fifth as infectious as someone with varicella.
secularTrendsSummary: About 1 million zoster episodes occur annually in the US, with an estimated lifetime risk of at least 32% - about half of people who live to age 85 will have had it. Increasing age and cellular immunosuppression are the most important risk factors; rates are declining in both children under 18 and older adults. As of 2017, only 34.9% of adults 60 or older had ever received a zoster vaccine.
vaccineDescription: RZV (Shingrix), a recombinant subunit vaccine containing glycoprotein E with a novel adjuvant (AS01B), is now the only zoster vaccine licensed and available in the US. ZVL (Zostavax), a live attenuated vaccine used from 2006, was discontinued for US distribution in 2020. RZV is given by intramuscular injection, contains no antibiotic or preservative, and - because it is not a live vaccine - cannot cause varicella.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: RZV is a 2-dose series for immunocompetent adults 50 years or older, with dose 2 given 2-6 months after dose 1. If more than 6 months elapse between doses, the series does not need to restart; a second dose given less than 4 weeks after the first, however, should be repeated. RZV is recommended regardless of prior ZVL or varicella vaccination, or a prior history of shingles, and adults 50 or older do not need to be screened for varicella history before vaccination.
vaccineEfficacySummary: In a phase III trial of more than 30,000 participants, efficacy against herpes zoster after more than 3 years was 96.6% for ages 50-59, 97.4% for ages 60-69, and 91.3% for ages 70 and older; pooled efficacy against PHN was 91.2% for ages 50+ and 88.8% for ages 70+. Because RZV's efficacy is both higher than ZVL's and does not wane as much over the following 4 years, ACIP issued a preferential recommendation for RZV over ZVL in 2017, while both were still in use.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication. Moderate or severe acute illness and pregnancy are precautions - there is no safety data for pregnant or lactating women and no ACIP recommendation for use in that population, so delaying until after delivery and lactation should be considered. ACIP has not yet made a recommendation for people on moderate- to high-dose immunosuppressive therapy, since they were excluded from the efficacy trials, but RZV IS recommended for people on low-dose immunosuppressive therapy (e.g. under 20 mg/day of prednisone or equivalent, or inhaled/topical steroids) and for those anticipating immunosuppression or recovering from an immunocompromising illness. People with a history of shingles should still be vaccinated, though an active acute episode should resolve first.
vaccineSafetySummary: Across two placebo-controlled trials (29,305 subjects), the most common reactions were injection-site pain (78%), myalgia (45%), and fatigue (45%). Grade 3 (severe but not life-threatening) adverse events were reported by 16.5% of vaccine recipients versus 3.1% of placebo recipients; grade 3 systemic reactions were more common after dose 2 than dose 1. A postmarketing observational study found an increased risk of Guillain-Barre syndrome in the 42 days following vaccination in adults 65 and older; FDA determined there is an association, though available evidence is insufficient to establish causation, added a GBS warning to the prescribing information, and concluded the vaccine's benefits continue to outweigh its risks - vaccination recommendations were not changed.
vaccineStorageSummary: Before reconstitution, store both the lyophilized antigen and the adjuvant suspension refrigerated at 2C to 8C (36F to 46F), protected from light. After reconstitution, use immediately or store refrigerated at 2C to 8C; discard if not used within 6 hours or if frozen.
surveillanceSummary: Unlike most other diseases in this library, zoster is NOT a nationally notifiable condition in the US. Diagnosis is usually clinical; when laboratory testing is needed (e.g. atypical presentation in an immunocompromised patient), PCR for VZV DNA on swabs of unroofed vesicles or crusted-lesion scabs is the most useful test, though a positive result cannot distinguish zoster from varicella. Direct fluorescent antibody testing and the Tzanck smear are not recommended due to limited sensitivity. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for general reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Switching from ZVL to RZV
supplementalTopics.summary: Zostavax (ZVL), the live-attenuated vaccine used from 2006 until its 2020 discontinuation, has been fully replaced by Shingrix (RZV). Anyone previously vaccinated with ZVL should still receive the full 2-dose RZV series. Intervals shorter than 5 years between ZVL and RZV have not been formally studied, but there's no known safety or effectiveness concern with a shorter gap; expert opinion recommends waiting at least 2 months after ZVL before giving RZV, and providers may weigh how old the patient was when they received ZVL, since ZVL is known to be less effective when given at 70 or older.

supplementalTopics.title: Postexposure Considerations
supplementalTopics.summary: Exposure to someone with varicella or zoster does not cause zoster in a susceptible contact - it causes varicella. Zoster vaccine therefore has no postexposure role and should not be used for that purpose; an exposed person without evidence of varicella immunity should instead receive varicella vaccine (within 3, possibly up to 5, days of exposure) or, if that's contraindicated, varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG). Unlike varicella vaccination, RZV requires no assessment of prior varicella history at all - it's recommended for essentially all immunocompetent adults 50 and older regardless of chickenpox or shingles history.

keyPoints: The term 'herpes zoster' dates to the encyclopedist Celsus (c. 25 BCE - c. 50 AD), but reactivation of latent VZV wasn't hypothesized as the cause until 1965
About 1 in 3 people in the US will develop zoster in their lifetime; risk rises sharply with age
Exposure to a person with zoster causes varicella, not zoster, in a susceptible contact - zoster is never 'caught' from someone else
Shingrix (RZV), a recombinant subunit vaccine, has fully replaced the live-attenuated Zostavax (ZVL), discontinued for US distribution in 2020
No screening for prior varicella history is needed before RZV vaccination, unlike the varicella vaccine itself
FDA has flagged an association (not established as causal) between Shingrix and Guillain-Barre syndrome in adults 65+, but vaccination recommendations are unchanged
Zoster is not a nationally notifiable condition in the US, unlike most other diseases in this library
